newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn govt urges building sector to accept pay deal.
newsitem.headline: Bonn govt urges building sector to accept pay deal.

text.p: The German government on Friday urged the construction industry unions and employers to accept a controversial wage deal because a strike would be "poison" for the sector.

Construction minister Klaus Toepfer said the deal, which cuts sick pay by 20 percent and raises pay by less than the rate of inflation, was "socially acceptable and economically sensible" given current conditions in the industry.

He noted that new building orders in Germany had fallen by 8.7 percent in January and February. "If I look at that then a labour dispute in such a situation would of course be poison," Toepfer said in a radio interview.

The agreement, reached in the early hours of Thursday after 20 hours of arbitration talks, falls far short of what the two sides were demanding. The two sides must agree within 14 days whether to accept the deal.

Under the deal, workers' pay will be cut by 20 percent during the first three weeks of sickness, wages for west Germany's 1.3 million workers will be increased by 1.3 percent from last April 1 and Christmas bonuses will also be cut. German inflation stands at about 1.5 percent.
The IG Bau trade union had, among other demands, called for wage increase of 2.9 percent and continued full pay during sick leave while employers had sought to keep pay unchanged.
Officials on both sides are sceptical whether the leadership of the industry employer group or the IG Bau union will approve the deal, which was reached by just five votes to four against.

Two representatives from the employers and two from IG Bau voted against the agreement. The two sides now have 14 days to decide whether to give the agreement their final approval. If they do not, IG Bau can lawfully call a strike.
IG Bau leader Klaus Wiesenhuegel said he was concerned the reduced sick-pay benefits would be rejected by union members.

Heiner Geissler, the senior politician from Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats who brokered the talks, said a collapse of the agreement "would be the worst that could happen to the construction sector."

Geissler told German radio he feared the deal may be rejected but added that negotiators could not have achieved a better agreement since tens of thousands of small building firms were already in financial trouble.

The wage accord also cuts the Christmas bonus or so-called "13th month" salary to about 77 percent of a month's salary and establishes a new lower wage group to create new jobs at a time of record German unemployment.
